chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
title: The guitar in the 1930s; playing at the mike with Ellington
summary: Guitar and tiple groups were unusual, banjo was fading, and with Duke he held the guitar up near the microphone.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Yeah. We got everything down. I guess at that time there weren't that many people, groups, that were featuring guitar, were there?
Was That was one of the unique things?
Yeah. But guitar wasn't as popular as it is today.
There's still a lot of -- the banjo is kind of going out?
And the guitar was coming in.
I You didn't hear too many banjos, period.
And the guitar was the leading thing then. And all them over in Honolulu was doing them ukuleles.
Right. It was hard for the guitar to play in the orchestra though, right? In the bigger bands,
I noticed that most of your playing, besides with the Spirits, where you had a chance to-- well, it was really a guitar group, you know.
When I was with Duke, I used to get up to the mike like this, you know, standing --
Two or three inches from the mike.
Just enough room to get your fingers clear of the --
How about in live performance? Did they have a mike, a PA system, or --
Yeah, they had a PA system.
The singers used microphones with Duke?
And the same thing, you would kind of come up to the front?
Yeah. I had to come up front.
Of course, a lot of that is up to the band.
Yeah. They can't overwhelm me, see, when I was up there doing my solos.
They had to cut it down. And I mean, they was very (unintelligible), you know.
They worked a lot with mutes and stuff anyway.
